title: The Fellowship of the Ring book release
phrase: the release of the book The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring
description: "Don't adventures ever have an end? I suppose not. Someone else always has to carry on the story."

title: The Two Towers book release
phrase: the release of the book The Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers
description: "I would not take this thing, if it lay by the highway. Not were Minas Tirith falling in ruin and I alone could save her, so, using the weapon of the Dark Lord for her good and my glory. No, I do not wish for such triumphs, Frodo." —Faramir. The book version of Faramir was far more level headed and wise.

title: The Return of the King book release
phrase: the release of the book The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King
description: Unlike the movies, the books contain the critically and thematically important "scouring of the Shire" which contextualizes the effects of the larger adventure. Frodo, Sam, Merry, and Pippin return to the Shire to find it under the control of an authoritarian regime that has torn down the old houses and replaced the mill with machinery that pollutes the air and water. They inspire and lead an uprising to overthrow those in power and restore the Shire. If you've only ever seen the movies, you should at least read this section of the books.

title: The narrator's day in Innsmouth in The Shadow over Innsmouth
phrase: the narrator's day in Innsmouth
description: "Disliking the dinginess of the single restaurant I had seen, I bought a fair supply of cheese crackers and ginger wafers to serve as a lunch later on." Cheez-Its were launched in 1921 so the narrator could plausibly be referring to them. Despite the power of cheese crackers the narrator fled before dawn on July 16. Lovecraft's horror of racial mixing absolutely influenced the story.

title: Diamond Sutra printed
phrase: the printing of the Diamond Sutra
description: This woodblock-printed scroll of a Buddhist sutra is broadly considered the oldest surviving printed book. It was walled up in the Mogao Caves near Dunhuang and found there in 1900. Its colophon says it was "reverently made for universal free distribution by Wang Jie on behalf of his two parents," the first known public domain dedication.

title: Earliest surviving edition of Journey to the West
phrase: the earliest surviving edition of Journey to the West
description: A fantastic retelling of the monk Xuanzang's real 7th-century pilgrimage to India for Buddhist scriptures, with Sun Wukong, a monkey born from a stone who learns 72 transformations. This Nanjing edition is the oldest copy left; two earlier editions are lost.

title: Don Quixote published
phrase: the publication of Don Quixote
description: Miguel de Cervantes's would-be knight attacks windmills he believes are giants, which gave us "tilting at windmills." It's often called the first modern novel. A writer calling himself Avellaneda beat Cervantes to a Part Two with a spurious one, so the real Part Two (1615) ends by insisting that any further books about Don Quixote would be spurious too.

title: Shakespeare's First Folio published
phrase: the publication of Shakespeare's First Folio
description: Seven years after Shakespeare died, his fellow actors John Heminges and Henry Condell collected 36 of his plays. Eighteen of them, including Macbeth, The Tempest, and Twelfth Night, aren't known to have been printed before.

title: Samuel Johnson's Dictionary published
phrase: the publication of Samuel Johnson's Dictionary
description: Johnson claimed he could write it in three years. It took seven, and he did it single-handedly, with clerks only to copy out quotations. Some definitions are opinions: a lexicographer is "a harmless drudge," and oats are "a grain which in England is generally given to horses, but in Scotland supports the people."

title: Grimms' Fairy Tales published
phrase: the publication of Grimms' Fairy Tales
description: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm called their collection Children's and Household Tales, and critics said it wasn't suitable for children. Later editions toned it down: the wicked mothers in Snow White and Hansel and Gretel became stepmothers, and Rapunzel stopped asking why her dress was getting tight.

title: Pride and Prejudice published
phrase: the publication of Pride and Prejudice
description: Jane Austen asked for £150 and sold the copyright to Thomas Egerton for £110. Like all her novels, it was published anonymously.

title: Frankenstein published
phrase: the publication of Frankenstein
description: In the cold, rainy "Year Without a Summer" after Mount Tambora erupted, Lord Byron suggested that he, Mary and Percy Shelley, and John Polidori each write a ghost story. Mary was 18. Her story, published anonymously, is one of the first science fiction novels.

title: Sequoyah completes the Cherokee syllabary
phrase: Sequoyah's completion of the Cherokee syllabary
description: Sequoyah couldn't read or write when he set out to give Cherokee a written form, and he settled on a symbol for each syllable, 86 in all. By 1825 most Cherokees could read and write in it, and the Cherokee Phoenix newspaper was printed in it.

title: Champollion presents the decipherment of hieroglyphs
phrase: Champollion's presentation of how to read hieroglyphs
description: Two weeks earlier, Jean-François Champollion had worked out that hieroglyphs were partly phonetic, shouted "Je tiens l'affaire!" ("I've got it!"), and fainted. On this day he showed his findings to a packed room at the Académie des Inscriptions et Belles-Lettres.

title: A Christmas Carol published
phrase: the publication of A Christmas Carol
description: Charles Dickens wrote it in six weeks, and the first edition sold out by Christmas Eve. A pirated copy appeared in January, and when Dickens sued, the pirates went bankrupt, which shrank his small profits even further.

title: Moby-Dick published
phrase: the publication of Moby-Dick
description: It came out in London first, and the British edition lacked the epilogue, so reviewers wondered how a narrator who went down with the ship was telling the story. It was a commercial failure and out of print when Herman Melville died in 1891.

title: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland published
phrase: the publication of Alice's Adventures in Wonderland
description: Lewis Carroll made the story up on July 4, 1862, rowing up the river Isis with the three young Liddell sisters, and Alice Liddell asked him to write it down. Carroll scrapped the first print run because the illustrator, John Tenniel, was unhappy with the printing.

title: First installment of the Oxford English Dictionary
phrase: the first installment of the Oxford English Dictionary
description: The first part was 352 pages and covered A to Ant. The editors hoped to finish in ten years, and the last part, Wise to the end of W, came out 44 years later. One especially prolific volunteer, the American surgeon W. C. Minor, sent in his quotation slips from Broadmoor Asylum.

title: Sherlock Holmes first appears
phrase: the first appearance of Sherlock Holmes
description: A Study in Scarlet ran in Beeton's Christmas Annual after many rejections. Arthur Conan Doyle pressed for a royalty and got £25 for the full rights instead.

title: Dracula published
phrase: the publication of Dracula
description: Bram Stoker told the story entirely through letters, diary entries, and newspaper articles. He originally set it in Styria, not Transylvania.

title: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz published
phrase: the publication of the book The Wonderful Wizard of Oz
description: L. Frank Baum's story of Dorothy and Toto, illustrated by W. W. Denslow, had a first printing of 10,000 copies and had sold three million by 1956. Dorothy's shoes are silver. The 1939 movie made them ruby.

title: The Marvelous Land of Oz published
phrase: the publication of The Marvelous Land of Oz
description: The first Oz sequel, and Dorothy isn't in it. The Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman got the big parts because they'd been the stars of the 1902 stage play. It introduces Princess Ozma and Jack Pumpkinhead.

title: Ozma of Oz published
phrase: the publication of Ozma of Oz
description: Dorothy returns, along with a talking yellow hen she names Billina. They meet Tik-Tok, a clockwork man and one of the first intelligent humanoid automata in literature.

title: The Emerald City of Oz published
phrase: the publication of The Emerald City of Oz
description: Baum meant this to be the last Oz book. Dorothy moves to Oz for good with Uncle Henry and Aunt Em, and Glinda makes Oz invisible to the outside world. Money troubles brought him back three years later, with eight more Oz books to come.

title: Glinda of Oz published
phrase: the publication of Glinda of Oz
description: Baum's fourteenth and final Oz book came out a year after he died. Other authors kept the series going, especially Ruth Plumly Thompson, who wrote 21 more.

title: Winnie-the-Pooh published
phrase: the publication of Winnie-the-Pooh
description: A. A. Milne's stories star the stuffed animals of his son, Christopher Robin, who named his teddy bear after Winnie, a Canadian black bear he often saw at London Zoo.

title: First Penguin paperbacks
phrase: the launch of Penguin paperbacks
description: Allen Lane said the poor reading on offer at Exeter's railway station inspired him. Penguins cost sixpence, the price of a pack of cigarettes, and were sold at Woolworths. Ten months later, a million had been printed.

title: The Hobbit published
phrase: the publication of The Hobbit
description: J. R. R. Tolkien was marking exam papers when he found a blank page and wrote, "In a hole in the ground there lived a hobbit." Once Bilbo's ring became the One Ring, Tolkien revised the second edition so Gollum turned aggressive and was distraught at losing it.

title: The Little Prince published
phrase: the publication of The Little Prince
description: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry wrote and illustrated it while living in New York, and it came out in the US first, in English and French. It's been translated into 600 languages and dialects, more than any book but the Bible.

title: Nineteen Eighty-Four published
phrase: the publication of Nineteen Eighty-Four
description: George Orwell wrote much of it on the Scottish island of Jura and finished the first draft in bed, shortly before he was diagnosed with tuberculosis. It gave English Big Brother, doublethink, thoughtcrime, and Newspeak.

title: Linear B deciphered
phrase: the decipherment of Linear B
description: As a 14-year-old schoolboy, Michael Ventris heard Arthur Evans, the excavator of Knossos, give a lecture. Building on Alice Kober's research, Ventris, an architect, showed that the script was Mycenaean Greek, the earliest known form of Greek, and announced it in a BBC radio talk.

title: The Cat in the Hat published
phrase: the publication of The Cat in the Hat
description: After John Hersey complained in Life that school primers like Dick and Jane were dull, Dr. Seuss was challenged: "Write me a story that first-graders can't put down!" He had to stick to a list of easy words, and the finished book uses 236 different ones.

title: Things Fall Apart published
phrase: the publication of Things Fall Apart
description: Chinua Achebe's first novel follows Okonkwo, an Igbo leader, as British missionaries and colonial rule arrive. Achebe decided to become a writer after reading Joyce Cary's Mister Johnson, which portrayed its Nigerian characters as savages or buffoons.

title: One Hundred Years of Solitude published
phrase: the publication of One Hundred Years of Solitude
description: Driving his family to Acapulco on vacation, Gabriel García Márquez thought of how the book should begin, turned the car around, and went home to Mexico City to write it. It follows generations of the Buendía family in Macondo, a town inspired by his childhood home, and has sold more than 50 million copies.

title: Project Gutenberg begins
phrase: the start of Project Gutenberg
description: On the Fourth of July, Michael Hart, a student at the University of Illinois, typed the US Declaration of Independence into a computer on the ARPANET and shared it. It was the first book in what's now the oldest digital library.

title: The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy published
phrase: the publication of the novel The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy
description: Douglas Adams adapted it from his radio comedy series. The supercomputer Deep Thought works out the answer to the Ultimate Question of Life, the Universe, and Everything: 42. Unfortunately, nobody knows what the question is.

title: Neuromancer published
phrase: the publication of Neuromancer
description: William Gibson's debut novel popularized cyberspace and "jacking in" and set the vocabulary of cyberpunk. It's still the only novel to win the Hugo, the Nebula, and the Philip K. Dick Award.

title: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone published
phrase: the publication of Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone
description: Most publishers thought it was too long at about 90,000 words. Bloomsbury took it and printed 500 copies, 300 of which went to libraries. In the US, Scholastic thought "philosopher" sounded too archaic and called it the Sorcerer's Stone.

title: Snow Crash published
phrase: the publication of Snow Crash
description: Neal Stephenson's hero, Hiro Protagonist, is a freelance hacker and a pizza delivery driver for the Mafia. The book coined "the Metaverse" and popularized "avatar" for a body online. Its title is Stephenson's name for the static-like gibberish an early Macintosh showed when it crashed.
